title: The Other AI
author: Dr. Megan Schopp
summary: Megan Schopp opens with her South Dakota rancher father, for whom AI has always meant artificial insemination, to show that rural communities already live with data-driven technology and hold varied, reasonable views of the letters. She then surveys what research says about AI in rural schools: rural teachers use AI about as much as urban ones, but rural districts lag on training and policy, a gap that tracks poverty more than geography. The evidence on student learning is mixed, with purpose-built tutors and human oversight helping and general chatbots bolted onto courses showing displaced engagement and no gains in a large new trial. Schopp weighs each rural benefit against its twin risk, such as access versus dependence and capacity versus fragility, and argues that out-of-field teaching and staffing shortages lower the bar for what AI must beat. Her central point is that the tool is never the real question, but who is still on the place when the tool is done.
points: Rural teachers are not behind on AI use; the gap is in training and written policy, and it follows district poverty more than rurality.
The studies showing real gains used curriculum-anchored tutors with humans in the loop, while a general chatbot dropped into a course displaced engagement without raising performance.
For a one-math-teacher rural high school, a purpose-built tutor can extend reach to courses the school cannot staff, which is the strongest case for AI there.
Rural leaders mainly want AI to relieve role compression through paperwork, grant narratives, and newsletters so adults can spend time knowing kids, not to replace teachers.
Sustainability is fragile when adoption depends on one person going above and beyond, so district-level scaffolding and policy matter more than any single tool.
quotes: The tool is never the question. The question is who is still here when the tool is done.
Where rural districts lag is not use. It is scaffolding around use.
The kids are using it. The schools are the ones without a plan.

The pattern across all of it is consistent. AI helps when it is purpose-built, anchored to the curriculum, and has a human in the loop. A general chatbot dropped into a course does not, and the general chatbot is what most teachers are using.
A purpose-built tutor that can walk a student through the second half of a calculus sequence the school cannot staff is not a luxury.
When 44% of rural applicants in a national scan name role compression as the problem they want solved, they are not asking for a robot teacher.

the honest comparison is not AI versus a certified physics teacher. It is AI supported instruction from an out-of-field teacher versus unsupported instruction from an out-of-field teacher, or no section at all.

What they share is that the national conversation about AI in education was not written with any of them in mind, and that the people who live in them are not waiting to be told what the letters mean.
